title: Financial literacy and sustainable planning assessment among Filipino millennials
authors: Dimaunahan, D. S. F.; Santiago, A. F. B.; Eusebio, M. C. C.; Loterina, S. M. M.; Ong, A. K. S.; Chavez, J. X. S.
tldr: Low financial literacy among Filipino millennials does not significantly predict financial planning behavior, while demographic factors and goal-setting mechanisms show substantial influence.
problem_and_motivation: There is a gap in low financial literacy levels and poor financial decision-making among Filipinos, with limited publicly available studies on millennial financial literacy in the Philippines particularly in relation to financial planning. The study addresses this gap by assessing the financial literacy of Filipino millennials and its influence on financial planning using goal-setting theory as a framework. The research seeks to understand why financial literacy remains low despite economic development and how demographic factors shape planning behavior.
approach: Correlational research method with 400 Filipino millennial respondents from Makati City.
Non-probability purposive sampling through online and in-person surveys over two months.
The Big Three financial literacy questions measuring interest compounding, inflation, and risk diversification.
Structural equation modeling using partial least squares (PLS-SEM) for data analysis.
Goal Setting Theory framework with four moderators: commitment, specificity, acceptance, and difficulty.
Demographic factors including monthly income, occupation, and monthly expenses as lower-order constructs.
findings: num: Financial literacy showed insignificant direct effect on financial planning (β = 0.077, p = 0.153).
num: Monthly expenses had strongest demographic effect on planning (β = 0.205, p = 0.001).
num: Goal acceptance was strongest predictor of financial planning (β = 0.924, p < 0.001).
num: Goal commitment showed significant effect (β = 0.809, p < 0.001) on planning behavior.
num: Interest compounding correct answer rate was 0.545, inflation 0.388, risk diversification 0.338.
Monthly income significantly influences financial planning (β = 0.180, p = 0.003).
Occupation significantly affects planning behavior (β = 0.164, p = 0.004).
Goal specificity contributes to planning (β = 0.597, p < 0.001) through clear objective setting.
Goal difficulty showed modest but significant effect (β = 0.212, p < 0.001).

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This study contributes evidence that financial literacy alone does not significantly predict financial planning behavior among Filipino millennials, challenging assumptions that literacy programs automatically improve planning. The research establishes that demographic factors like income, occupation, and expenses, combined with goal-setting mechanisms, are stronger predictors of planning behavior. The application of Goal Setting Theory to Philippine financial context provides a validated framework for understanding financial planning drivers. The findings suggest that financial capability interventions should focus on goal-setting practices and economic empowerment rather than literacy education alone.
directly_justifies: Financial literacy shows insignificant effect on financial planning (β = 0.077, p = 0.153).
Monthly expenses demonstrate strongest demographic effect (β = 0.205, p = 0.001).
Goal acceptance is strongest predictor with β = 0.924 (p < 0.001).
Only 33.8% of respondents correctly answered risk diversification question.
71.3% of respondents are employed full-time with 67.6% holding bachelor's degrees.
limits: Geographic focus limited to Makati City urban area not representative of entire Philippines.
Sample restricted to millennials only excluding other age groups for comparison.
Single financial literacy measure (Big Three) may not capture comprehensive literacy.
Cross-sectional design cannot establish causal relationships over time.
Correlational method limits causal inference despite SEM approach.
Self-reported data introduces potential response biases and social desirability effects.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all topic domains identified primary relevance in domains 1 (Filipino demographics and behavior) and 7 (budgeting strategies). Domain 1.A is highly relevant as it profiles Filipino millennials including income, employment, and education characteristics. Domain 1.C is highly relevant through assessment of financial literacy and planning behaviors. Domain 7.A is moderately relevant for examining financial planning as a structured resource allocation strategy. Domain 12.B has low relevance through SEM evaluation methodology. Domains 2-6 (cultural practices, expense categorization, existing systems, behavioral profiles, forecasting) were considered but rejected as not directly addressed. Domains 8-11 (anomaly detection, mobile design, privacy, engagement) were considered and rejected as not covered. Domain 13 (savings/debt management) was considered but rejected as the study focuses on planning rather than specific saving or debt behaviors. Domain 14 (synthetic data) was considered but rejected as real survey data is used.
limitations: Urban Makati City focus limits generalizability to rural and other Philippine regions.
Millennial-only sample excludes comparative analysis across generations.
Big Three questions provide benchmark but not comprehensive financial literacy assessment.
Cross-sectional design cannot observe how planning behavior evolves over time.
Correlational approach prevents causal conclusions despite sophisticated SEM analysis.
Self-report methodology may inflate responsible behaviors through social desirability.

remember_this: Financial literacy shows insignificant effect on financial planning among Filipino millennials.
Goal acceptance is the strongest predictor of financial planning behavior (β = 0.924).
Monthly expenses, income, and occupation all significantly influence planning behavior.
Only 33.8% correctly answered risk diversification question indicating low literacy.
Demographic factors matter more than literacy for financial planning outcomes.
